transcript.text: Our hospital wants to predict at the moment of patient discharge whether a patient will be readmitted within 30 days. Because of HIPAA privacy rules we cannot upload patient records. We discharge 3,000 patients a month with a 12% readmission rate; a follow-up nurse visit costs $80 and avoids a $1,600 penalty.

# A solution designed without data

## The problem

The hospital needs to decide, at the moment of discharge, which patients should receive a follow-up nurse visit to avoid a 30-day readmission penalty.

Who makes the decision: the discharge team, transition-of-care manager, or follow-up nurse assignment process.

When: at discharge, before the 30-day outcome is known.

Unit: one patient discharge encounter.

What the person told us:
- The hospital discharges `3,000` patients a month.
- The readmission rate is `12%`.
- A follow-up nurse visit costs `$80`.
- The penalty avoided is `$1,600`.
- The prediction target is readmission within 30 days of discharge.
- HIPAA privacy rules prevent uploading patient records.

What is not known:
- The exact definition of the readmission that triggers the penalty.
- Whether the nurse visit prevents readmission, prevents only the penalty, or prevents a subset of penalties.
- Current follow-up capacity.
- Current practice: who already receives follow-up visits.
- Which fields are reliably available at discharge.
- How long after discharge the label and penalty are known in internal billing or claims data.

## What needs care

The model must not use anything that is only known after discharge as a prediction input. The decision is made at discharge, so age, diagnoses, prior admissions, and current measurements must be available at that moment.

The business question is not only “Will this patient be readmitted?” but “Which follow-up visits avoid enough penalties to pay for themselves?”

The cost-benefit floor is direct: one follow-up visit costs `$80`, and one avoided penalty is worth `$1,600`. So, if an action avoids the whole penalty, the follow-up must succeed on at least `80 / 1,600 = 5%` of the patients who receive it for the action’s cost to be covered.

The overall readmission rate gives scale, not success by itself:
- `3,000 × 12% = 360` readmission cases occur per month at the stated rate.
- If every discharge received a nurse visit, the visit cost would be `3,000 × 80 = 240,000`.
- If every readmission case were caught and every catch avoided the penalty, the maximum possible avoided penalty would be `3,000 × 12% × 1,600 = 576,000`.
- The maximum theoretical net gain would be `576,000 - 240,000 = 336,000`, but only if every visit truly avoided a penalty. The real net gain depends on follow-up effectiveness and is not known.

No patient record upload is asked for. The work can be designed for the hospital’s secure internal environment.

## Business solution

Start without a model by testing the economics of the existing follow-up process.

Action:
- Use the current discharge process to identify patients who are already considered high risk, or who already receive follow-up visits.
- Track two numbers for that group: visits performed and penalties avoided.
- Calculate whether the avoided-penalty rate among visits reaches `80 / 1,600 = 5%`.

Simple rule:
- If follow-up visits avoid penalties on at least 5% of the visits given, the action is cost-covered at the stated penalty value.
- If fewer than 5% of visits avoid penalties, the visit cost is not covered, and follow-up should be moved toward patients more likely to generate an avoided penalty.

If the hospital can staff all follow-up visits, the all-patient cost is known: `3,000 × 80 = 240,000`. The all-patient maximum possible avoided penalty is `3,000 × 12% × 1,600 = 576,000`. But that maximum assumes every follow-up visit prevents a penalty for every readmission case. That is not known until the visit effectiveness is measured.

A safe first business rule is capacity-limited and measured:
- Assign follow-up visits to the highest-risk patients from existing discharge checklists, prior readmission history, or clinical concern.
- Then compare those visits with not receiving a follow-up, using the same penalty definition.
- Expand only if the measured share of avoided penalties among follow-up visits is above `80 / 1,600 = 5%`, or if clinical policy requires the visit for reasons beyond penalty avoidance.

## Data to record

| column | what it is | known when | role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `discharge_encounter_id` | Unique identifier for each discharge encounter | at | key |
| `discharge_date_time` | Exact time the patient is discharged and the follow-up decision is made | at | time |
| `age` | Patient age at discharge | at | input |
| `sex_or_gender` | Recorded sex or gender at discharge | at | input |
| `primary_diagnosis_code` | Primary diagnosis coded at discharge | at | input |
| `comorbidity_flags` | Chronic or acute condition flags known at discharge | at | input |
| `prior_admission_count` | Number of prior hospital admissions before this discharge | before | input |
| `prior_30_day_readmission_count` | Number of prior 30-day readmissions before this discharge | before | input |
| `length_of_stay` | Current admission length at discharge | at | input |
| `discharge_service_or_team` | Medical, surgical, unit, or attending team at discharge | at | input |
| `discharge_labs_or_vitals` | Measurements recorded and available at discharge | at | input |
| `follow_up_nurse_assigned` | Whether a follow-up nurse visit was assigned at discharge | at | not used |
| `follow_up_nurse_completed` | Whether the follow-up nurse visit occurred after discharge | after | not used |
| `readmission_date_time` | Date and time of the next readmission after discharge, if any | after | not used |
| `readmitted_within_30_days` | Whether a qualifying readmission occurred within 30 days after discharge | after | label |
| `penalty_incurred` | Whether the `$1,600` penalty was triggered for this discharge outcome | after | label |

- One row is one discharge encounter for one patient.
- The decision moment is the discharge time, when the follow-up nurse visit is assigned or not assigned.
- The primary label is `readmitted_within_30_days`: it is counted from `discharge_date_time`, is known only after 30 days from discharge, and may become known later if claims, billing, or readmission data have reporting lag.

## Model

Simple baseline first:
- Baseline 1: assign no follow-up visits, so avoided-penalty value is `$0` and visit cost is `$0`.
- Baseline 2: assign follow-up visits to all patients, cost is `3,000 × 80 = 240,000` per month at the stated volume.
- Baseline 3: assign follow-up visits using the existing discharge checklist or current clinical risk flags.
- Constant-rate baseline: use the current overall `12%` readmission rate for every discharge. This is useful only as a reference; it does not rank patients.

Model design:
- Target: `readmitted_within_30_days`, a binary outcome.
- Training data: only columns known `before` or `at` the discharge decision.
- Exclude from inputs: `follow_up_nurse_completed`, `readmission_date_time`, `readmitted_within_30_days`, `penalty_incurred`, and any after-discharge notes.
- Start with a simple interpretable model, such as logistic regression or a gradient-boosted tree model, inside the hospital’s secure environment.
- If the hospital already uses structured risk flags, include those flags as inputs only if they are available at discharge.

Testing:
- Split by time, not randomly. Train on earlier discharge months and validate on later discharge months. This prevents the model from using future clinical practice patterns as hidden information.
- Use calibration and decision-oriented measures, not only classification accuracy. Calibration matters because the model’s probability must be converted into expected penalty avoidance.
- Business measure: for a validation month, compute avoided-penalty value from actual labels and follow-up effects, then subtract visit cost.

Decision rule from score:
- The model outputs predicted readmission probability `p`.
- The follow-up visit’s probability of avoiding the penalty, conditional on a readmission-prone patient, is unknown from the statement alone. Call it effectiveness `e`.
- Expected avoided penalty per followed patient is `p × e × 1,600`.
- Expected net value per followed patient is `p × e × 1,600 - 80`.
- Follow up a patient when the expected avoided penalty exceeds the visit cost: `p × e × 1,600 > 80`, equivalently `p × e > 80 / 1,600 = 5%`.

If `e` is not known, do not assume the raw readmission probability can be thresholded at 5%. First measure `e` in a limited follow-up cohort, or use a conservative capacity-limited pilot on the highest-score patients and compare avoided penalties against visit costs.

Kind: binary supervised classification with a 30-day outcome horizon.

## Plan

1. Confirm the decision owner and action.  
   Done when a named discharge process owner agrees that follow-up assignment is made at discharge and that the visit can avoid the stated penalty under the hospital’s rules.

2. State the no-upload privacy rule.  
   Done when the hospital team agrees that no patient record is to be sent outside the secure environment and that modeling uses internal data only.

3. Confirm the penalty definition.  
   Done when the hospital agrees whether the `$1,600` penalty follows any qualifying 30-day readmission, a related readmission, a specific diagnosis, or another internal rule.

4. Build the recording table.  
   Done when the discharge system can create one row per discharge encounter and fill only `before` or `at` inputs at the decision moment.

5. Compute the no-model scale.  
   Done when the hospital can identify, for a recent period, the number of follow-up visits and avoided penalties so that the follow-up success share can be compared with `80 / 1,600 = 5%`.

6. Evaluate current follow-up practice.  
   Done when the hospital knows how many currently followed patients avoid penalties and how many do not, using the same penalty definition.

7. Create the label from historical outcomes.  
   Done when `readmitted_within_30_days` can be calculated from discharge time and readmission time, and the label lag is known.

8. Fit a simple baseline model.  
   Done when a logistic regression or tree-based model is trained in the secure environment using only discharge-time inputs.

9. Test by time.  
   Done when later discharge months are held out, and model probabilities are calibrated against observed readmission rates.

10. Convert scores into a follow-up rule.  
   Done when patients are assigned to follow-up only when the expected penalty avoided is above the visit cost, using measured effectiveness or a conservative pilot threshold.

11. Pilot and measure.  
   Done when the hospital can compare avoided penalties against visit cost for the pilot group and decide whether to expand, shrink, or change the rule.

## What only real data can settle

- The actual penalty trigger and whether the nurse visit prevents the penalty, the readmission, or both.
- The share of readmissions that carry the `$1,600` penalty under hospital and payer rules.
- The real effectiveness of follow-up visits, needed to set the correct model threshold.
- Which discharge-time fields are complete and meaningful enough to predict readmission.
- Whether the current follow-up process already avoids penalties above or below the `80 / 1,600 = 5%` break-even share.
- Whether model performance and calibration are strong enough to justify moving follow-up capacity to model-selected patients.

## Questions for you

1. What exactly triggers the `$1,600` penalty: any qualifying 30-day readmission, a readmission with a related diagnosis, a specific patient class, or an internal quality rule?

2. Does the follow-up nurse visit prevent the readmission, prevent the penalty after a readmission occurs, or prevent only a subset of penalties?

3. What follow-up capacity exists now, and who already receives follow-up visits?

## Checked by code
- Sums checked by code: `80 / 1,600 = 5%`; `3,000 × 12% = 360`; `3,000 × 80 = 240,000`; `3,000 × 12% × 1,600 = 576,000`; `576,000 - 240,000 = 336,000`.

## Checks DCLab will run when real data arrives
- `time_split_check` on `discharge_date_time`: Declared time column
- `grouped_split` on `discharge_encounter_id`: Declared entity key
- `baseline` on `roc_auc`: Baseline model

## A second reader's findings
- The plan says to compare patients who received follow-up visits with those who did not using current practice, but without controlled assignment the difference may reflect who was selected as high risk rather than whether the visit avoids the penalty; run a randomized or carefully matched pilot under the confirmed penalty rule before estimating visit effectiveness.
- It centers the prediction on `readmitted_within_30_days` although the hospital is paying $80 to avoid a $1,600 penalty, and it admits the penalty trigger may be narrower than any readmission; instead train on the label that actually causes the penalty, or confirm the penalty definition before treating readmission as the target.
- The score rule multiplies predicted readmission probability by unknown visit effectiveness, assuming the model's probability identifies the same patients for whom the visit can causally change the penalty outcome; instead estimate causal penalty avoidance from the pilot and use the measured effect to choose thresholds.
- It lists fields such as `primary_diagnosis_code` and `discharge_labs_or_vitals` as known at discharge, but final coding and some measurements may not be available when the follow-up decision is made; verify the actual fields available at the decision time in the discharge workflow before building the feature table.

transcript.text: We want to predict industrial compressor failure 7 days before breakdown across 1,200 factory machines, but we have not started logging sensor tables yet. A preventive inspection costs $120 and avoids $3,000 in unplanned downtime.

# A solution designed without data

## The problem
- Decision: which compressor(s) should receive a preventive inspection now, for a breakdown expected within the next 7 days.
- Who makes it and when: a reliability/maintenance planner, at each logging snapshot when the system must choose “inspect” or “do not inspect.”
- Unit: one machine/compressor at one decision snapshot.
- What you told me: 1,200 factory machines, preventive inspection costs $120, one prevented failure avoids $3,000 in unplanned downtime, and sensor tables are not being logged yet.
- What is not known: current failure frequency, machine criticality, maintenance history quality, available sensor channels, decision cadence, alerting capacity, whether an inspection fully prevents the downtime, and how failures are recorded.

## What needs care
- **The 7-day horizon must be real.** A model can only use data that was measured before or at the decision snapshot. Using sensor values recorded after or during the failure would make the prediction look unrealistically good.
- **The cost rule is strict.** Because each inspection costs $120 and each caught failure saves $3,000, 120 / 3,000 = 4%. In plain terms, at least 4% of the inspections that are triggered must find a failure that truly would have caused unplanned downtime, if the inspection fully avoids the cost.
- **Rare failures need careful evaluation.** A model that says “inspect everything” may look accurate but spends too much. The goal is to alert a smaller set with enough true failures inside it.
- **Inspection changes the outcome.** If an inspection prevents a breakdown, the actual downtime may not appear in the log. You need to record the decision, the inspection, and the reason it was performed, not only whether downtime happened.
- **No sensor history means no supervised model yet.** The first useful step is to start recording the right fields and create a simple manual rule while data accumulates.

## Business solution
- **Action now without a model:** create a manual warning-based inspection rule. Inspect only when there is a recorded reason that a compressor is abnormal or overdue for preventive work.
- **Simple rule to begin with:**
  - Inspect if an operator reports abnormal sound, heat, leak, smoke, vibration, pressure drift, or another warning at the decision moment.
  - Inspect if a maintenance system shows the compressor is overdue for preventive work or has a prior unplanned downtime record and high criticality.
  - Otherwise, do not inspect solely because it is one of the 1,200 machines.
- **Cost and gain in your numbers:** each inspection costs $120; each prevented failure avoids $3,000. The rule should be selective enough that its inspected set meets the 120 / 3,000 = 4% break-even precision. Inspecting every machine is too blunt unless the maintenance program can already justify it by cost and capacity.
- **Immediate business value:** this manual rule converts maintenance knowledge and operator warnings into a traceable decision log. That log becomes the foundation for the later model without requiring sensor data to exist first.

## Data to record

| column | what it is | known when | role |
|---|---|---|---|
| machine_id | unique compressor or factory machine identifier | before | key |
| snapshot_time | exact date/time when the inspection decision is made for this machine | at | time |
| target_start_time | start of the 7-day prediction window following the decision | at | not used |
| target_end_time | end of the 7-day prediction window following the decision | at | not used |
| breakdown_within_7_days | whether an unplanned compressor failure occurred during the 7-day window | after | label |
| actual_unplanned_downtime_cost | actual unplanned downtime cost observed during the window | after | not used |
| inspection_performed | whether a preventive inspection was performed after the decision | after | not used |
| failure_prevented | maintenance/operations judgment that an inspection prevented a likely failure, if this can be recorded without using after-the-fact data as a feature | after | not used |
| criticality_tier | machine criticality or production-line importance assigned before the decision | before | input |
| maintenance_overdue_flag | whether maintenance policy shows the machine is overdue for preventive work | before | input |
| operator_warning_flag | operator report of abnormal sound, heat, leak, smoke, vibration, or pressure behavior | before | input |
| alarm_flag | system/process alarm active just before or at the decision time | at | input |
| pressure_sensor_value | latest pressure reading or pressure average ending at the decision time | at | input |
| temperature_sensor_value | latest temperature reading or temperature average ending at the decision time | at | input |
| vibration_sensor_value | latest vibration reading or vibration aggregate ending at the decision time | at | input |
| current_load_value | motor current or load signal ending at the decision time | at | input |
| hours_since_last_service | running hours since the last completed service, from maintenance records | before | input |
| days_since_last_inspection | elapsed days since the last preventive inspection, from records | before | input |
| prior_unplanned_downtime_date | most recent past unplanned downtime date for the machine, if any | before | input |
| prior_inspection_result | finding from the last completed inspection | before | input |

- One row is one machine × one snapshot_time decision.
- The moment of the decision is snapshot_time, when reliability/maintenance chooses inspect or no inspect for the next 7 days.
- The label is breakdown_within_7_days: true if an unplanned compressor failure occurs between target_start_time and target_end_time; it is known after the 7-day window closes, or sooner if the incident report is completed during the window.

## Model
- **Baseline first:** start with the manual rule above, then test whether it is more cost-effective than no inspection or inspecting all machines.
- **Model once data exists:** use a supervised 7-day risk model, preferably calibrated logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees on the recorded before/at columns.
- **Testing:** split by time: train on earlier snapshots, then test on later snapshots. Also test machines that were not present in training, if machine variety is wide. Use precision, recall, calibration, and cost-based net value rather than accuracy alone.
- **Score to decision:** convert model risk into an inspection decision. If the model gives the probability that a failure will occur in the next 7 days, inspect when the expected saved cost exceeds the inspection cost. With the given numbers, that is when the risk exceeds 120 / 3,000 = 4%, assuming a successful inspection avoids the full $3,000 downtime cost.
- If inspection capacity is limited, rank machines by predicted risk and inspect the highest-ranked set only if that set meets a validated cost-effective precision level.

Kind: 7-day binary failure risk prediction

## Plan
1. **Define the failure event.** Agree what counts as an unplanned compressor failure worth $3,000 avoided downtime. Finished when the maintenance and operations teams approve one written label definition.
2. **Create the logging table.** Use the fields above as the schema. Finished when one machine snapshot can be saved with machine_id, snapshot_time, inputs, and later outcome fields.
3. **Start manual warning logging now.** Collect operator reports, alarms, overdue maintenance flags, and prior downtime dates for the 1,200 machines. Finished when every new inspection decision can be tied to a machine and decision time.
4. **Apply the simple inspection rule.** Inspect machines with operator warnings, active alarms, or overdue critical maintenance. Finished when inspections, non-inspections, and reasons are recorded daily or per decision cadence.
5. **Track outcomes through the 7-day window.** Record whether breakdowns occurred and the actual downtime cost. Finished when enough completed snapshots have both decision inputs and after-window outcomes.
6. **Build the first calibrated baseline model.** Fit a logistic model using only before/at fields and predict breakdown_within_7_days. Finished when the model produces a risk score for each machine snapshot without using after-window data.
7. **Backtest by time and cost.** Compare model alerts to the manual rule and no inspection using the business measure: prevented-failure value minus inspection cost. Finished when you know whether the model alert set passes the cost break-even test and what alert threshold is defensible.

## What only real data can settle
- The true failure rate and whether 7 days is a reliable warning window for your compressors.
- Whether sensor readings before failure differ clearly from normal operation.
- Whether preventive inspections actually avoid the full $3,000 downtime cost or only partially reduce it.
- How many alerts your maintenance team can handle and at what inspection capacity the cost rule changes.
- Whether different compressor models, lines, or criticality tiers need separate thresholds.
- Whether manual warnings, alarms, and maintenance history are strong enough before sensors are fully logged.

## Questions for you
1. What exact event counts as a failure that triggers the $3,000 avoided downtime cost?
2. How many preventive inspections can your team perform per decision window, if there is a limit?
3. Which non-sensor records already exist for these machines: maintenance work orders, operator warnings, alarms, or unplanned downtime reports?

## Checked by code
- Sums checked by code: `120 / 3,000 = 4%`; `1,200 × 120 = 144,000`.

## Checks DCLab will run when real data arrives
- `time_split_check` on `snapshot_time`: Declared time column
- `grouped_split` on `machine_id`: Declared entity key
- `leakage_probe` on `records`: Suspect post-outcome column name
- `baseline` on `roc_auc`: Baseline model

## A second reader's findings
- The model treats observed breakdowns within the 7-day window as the target, but inspections may prevent the failures that would have been counted, making the label biased by the maintenance decisions. Start with a decision log and a randomized or held-out no-inspection group, and only fit a supervised risk model after you can separate prevented failures from ordinary no-failure periods.
- It asks for pressure, temperature, vibration, current, alarm, and operator-warning values before breakdown even though no sensor tables exist and those channels or recording times are unknown. First inventory only fields that can truly be captured at the decision moment, define the failure event, and begin with a minimal maintenance/operator log.
- It assumes each inspection can avoid the full $3,000 and that the $120 cost alone sets a safe decision rule, without verifying inspection success, capacity, or the work caused by false warnings. Use $120/$3,000 as decision values only, then validate thresholds from real inspection outcomes and maintenance capacity.
- It spends effort on logistic or gradient models, time splits, and machine-variety testing while the immediate business gap is that there is no data and a rule is already available. Keep the first solution as selective manual inspections with traceable logging, and defer model building until enough trustworthy, decision-time fields exist.
We need to estimate the spot freight price per shipment at booking time before we have historical lane data.

# A solution designed without data

## The problem
The decision is whether a spot freight shipment can be booked, tendered, or quoted at an acceptable spot price before any historical lane-specific price record exists. The person making it is usually the pricing, booking, or procurement team, at the moment the customer requests a spot shipment or the carrier tender is released. The unit is a single shipment booking attempt, priced in the relevant currency and price components. The person has stated that the target is the spot freight price per shipment at booking time and that historical lane data is not available yet. Not known yet is the exact price target definition, the decision rules that should apply, the fields reliably available before the decision, and the guardrails that will separate automated from manual decisions.

## What needs care
A quick answer would be wrong if the model predicts the wrong target: customer revenue, carrier cost, or a market benchmark price. It would also be wrong if it uses information only available after the booking decision, such as the final carrier acceptance price or invoice. With no historical lane data, lane-specific patterns must be learned from comparable lanes, external market signals, and shipment attributes, not from lane history. Price components, currency, service type, equipment, and confirmation timing can differ enough to make a single average misleading. Spot pricing can move quickly, so the reference signal used must be current at the decision moment.

## Business solution
Start with a manual spot price reference worksheet and a simple comparable-shipment rule. For each booking attempt, search for the most recent confirmed comparable shipment or quote using origin metro, destination metro, equipment type, service level, and booking channel. If no comparable shipment exists, broaden the search progressively by origin/destination hub, port cluster, or similar lane group. If still unavailable, use the current external market index or published rate and adjust only for shipment attributes that are known before the decision.

The action is to make an estimate, record it, book or quote, then later compare the estimate with the confirmed price. The cost is the staff time the team already spends finding spot quotes, plus any cost of market-index or quote access. The gain is measured in your own records as the difference between your estimate and the confirmed spot price, plus the number of re-quotes or escalations your booking records already capture. This builds the label needed for a model without waiting for historical lane data.

## Data to record

| column | what it is | known when | role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| shipment_id | unique identifier for the shipment booking attempt | before | key |
| booking_ts | timestamp of the spot booking, quote, or tender decision | at | time |
| decision_type | spot booking process such as instant book, tendered spot, negotiated spot, or other | before | input |
| lane_id | normalized origin-destination lane or route grouping | before | input |
| origin_location | exact origin address, terminal, or location code | before | input |
| destination_location | exact destination address, terminal, or location code | before | input |
| origin_metro | metropolitan area, city, hub, or port cluster for origin | before | input |
| destination_metro | metropolitan area, city, hub, or port cluster for destination | before | input |
| origin_port | origin port or terminal if applicable | before | input |
| destination_port | destination port or terminal if applicable | before | input |
| equipment_type | truck, container, or other equipment required | before | input |
| weight_estimate | requested or estimated gross weight | before | input |
| volume_estimate | requested or estimated volume | before | input |
| packages_estimate | requested package count | before | input |
| dimensions_estimate | longest dimensions or dimensional weight | before | input |
| service_level | service tier or transit expectation | before | input |
| cargo_type | commodity class or cargo category | before | input |
| hazardous | hazard flag | before | input |
| pickup_date | requested pickup day | before | input |
| delivery_due_date | requested delivery day | before | input |
| distance | route distance | before | input |
| currency | currency used for the spot price request | before | not used |
| market_index_price | external spot index or published rate available at decision time | before | input |
| reference_quote_price | most recent comparable confirmed quote or price used by the manual rule | before | input |
| customer_price_limit | maximum customer-approved price, if provided | before | input |
| actual_spot_price | confirmed executed spot price for the shipment | after | label |
| accessorial_breakdown | components included in the confirmed price | after | not used |
| price_confirmation_ts | timestamp when the actual spot price becomes known | after | not used |
| carrier_id | carrier or service provider that ultimately accepted the shipment | after | not used |

Each row is a shipment quote or booking attempt. The decision moment is the timestamp when the spot price must be estimated for the customer quote, carrier tender, or internal booking. The label is the confirmed actual spot price for the same shipment; it becomes known after the decision when carrier confirmation, system pricing, or invoice posting provides it, with latency measured from the booking timestamp.

## Model
Begin with a simple baseline: the nearest comparable confirmed price. Start from the same origin metro, destination metro, equipment type, service level, and decision type; if that is unavailable, broaden similarity progressively by hub, port cluster, route group, or other known lane attributes. Use the market index only as a fallback or adjustment anchor, never as a substitute for the actual booking price.

Once confirmed booking labels exist, build a global cold-start regression model. It should predict actual_spot_price from shipment attributes, origin and destination features, lane similarity groups, distance, service level, cargo type, equipment, time features, and external market signals. Because lane history is absent, lane effects should be learned through broader lane groups, port or region features, and external lane characteristics, not through a unique lane identifier. When a lane eventually has history, add a lane-level correction by shrinking observed lane residuals back toward the global prediction.

Test the model on time, not on a random mixture: use older bookings to train and newer bookings to validate or test, because spot pricing drifts. Also simulate the cold-start problem by holding out complete lanes or lane groups and checking how well the global model predicts unseen lanes. Measure error with mean absolute error and mean absolute percentage error. If the model will be used with guardrails, also evaluate prediction intervals using quantile loss or a pinball-loss equivalent.

The score becomes the decision through your business limits. If the predicted price, plus its uncertainty, remains below your internal maximum acceptable cost or the customer limit, the estimate can be released automatically. If it is clearly above the limit, reject or escalate. If it falls close to the limit or uncertainty is wide, send it to manual review. The model does not replace the limit; it ranks, bounds, and reduces the need for manual spot research.

Kind: regression with cold-start and time-dependent pricing.

## Plan
1. Define the decision unit, target price, and label. This needs agreement from pricing or booking on whether the target is customer price, carrier cost, or market price. It is finished when the label definition and booking timestamp are written down.
2. Build the manual estimator worksheet. This needs current comparable quotes, market index access, shipment attributes, and your booking records. It is finished when staff can produce and record an estimate for each new booking attempt.
3. Record data from every real booking attempt using the table fields. This needs the booking system, quote record, and later confirmation or invoice data. It is finished when each attempt has an estimate row and an actual spot price label once confirmed.
4. Run the comparable-price baseline against confirmed labels. This needs labeled bookings and the manual estimate values. It is finished when estimate-to-actual differences are stored and reviewed.
5. Prepare cold-start features. This needs origin and destination normalization, metro or port groupings, distance calculation, equipment and service mapping, and external market signals. It is finished when a shipment without lane history can receive a feature row for prediction.
6. Train the global model once enough labeled bookings exist. This needs the recorded shipment fields and actual confirmed prices. It is finished when the model can produce estimates for unseen shipments and lane groups.
7. Add out-of-time validation and lane-group validation. This needs historical booking labels and lane or origin-destination groupings. It is finished when newer bookings and unseen lane groups are scored and errors are stored by segment.
8. Apply the model to booking decisions. This needs your internal price guardrails, customer limits if available, and a review workflow. It is finished when estimates are routed to automatic release, manual review, or rejection based on your existing limits.

# A solution designed without data

## The problem
The decision is how to place e-commerce buyers into behavioral cohorts so that lifecycle marketing can send each buyer a message, offer, or cadence that fits their buying state. The owner is the lifecycle or e-commerce marketing manager, with support from CRM, analytics, and campaign operations. The decision moment is the date when a buyer is assigned to a cohort for a campaign. The unit is the buyer, viewed as a snapshot of their behavior at that assignment date.

You told me that you want behavioral cohorts for tailored lifecycle marketing and that you do not have data ready to upload. That is enough to design the cohort logic, the data model, and the way the solution will later be tested. What remains unknown includes the fields already collected, the order and campaign history, the data windows you can use, the offers available, the cost of each offer, the current baseline response, privacy constraints, and how often you refresh cohorts.

## What needs care
- Cohort features must be known at the assignment date. A buyer’s future response, future spend, or later browsing cannot become a feature used before the campaign.
- Behavioral cohorts need to be operationally usable. A segment that is statistically interesting but cannot be routed to an offer, message, or owner will not help lifecycle marketing.
- “Behavioral” can include purchase history, browsing, email engagement, cart abandonment, returns, and channel preference. You should not overfit to one signal before you see the real data.
- If buyers move between cohorts frequently, campaigns may feel inconsistent. Cohort refresh logic needs to be explicit, not left to the model.

## Business solution
Start with a rule-based lifecycle segmentation before any model. Use the three core buyer signals that lifecycle teams can usually explain and act on: recency, frequency, and value.

A simple beginning rule is:

- Assign every buyer to a cohort as of the campaign decision date.
- Define recency by the gap between the last completed order and the assignment date.
- Define frequency by completed orders within a chosen pre-assignment lookback window.
- Define value by spend within a chosen pre-assignment lookback window or lifetime value, depending on what the business can act on.
- Create named cohorts such as active buyers, high-value buyers, at-risk buyers, lapsed buyers, and new buyers. The thresholds are unknown until you look at the real distribution, so begin with business-defined ranges or percentile-based ranges from available history.

The immediate action is to map each cohort to a lifecycle offer:

- Active high-value buyers: cross-sell, loyalty, early access, or premium bundles.
- Active lower-value buyers: upsell, category expansion, or modest incentives.
- At-risk buyers: winback, reminder, or reassurance message.
- Lapsed buyers: stronger reactivation offer, subject to cost and deliverability.
- New buyers: onboarding, first-purchase incentive, or education sequence.

The cost is the time needed to define cohort names, thresholds, data windows, and offer routing. The gain is not a guaranteed revenue figure without your baseline, but it is a better matching of offer and audience. The way to measure the gain is to compare next order, next spend, or campaign revenue for each cohort against the prior campaign baseline.

## Data to record

| column | what it is | known when | role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| buyer_id | Stable unique buyer identifier | before | key |
| cohort_assignment_date | Date the buyer is assigned to a cohort for a campaign | at | time |
| signup_date | Date the buyer created their account | before | time |
| first_order_date | Date of the buyer’s first completed order | before | time |
| last_order_date | Date of the most recent completed order as of assignment | at | time |
| days_since_last_order | Gap between last completed order and assignment date | at | input |
| order_count_in_lookback | Completed orders inside the chosen pre-assignment lookback | at | input |
| spend_in_lookback | Revenue from completed orders inside the chosen pre-assignment lookback | at | input |
| lifetime_spend | Total revenue from completed orders up to assignment | at | input |
| lifetime_order_count | Completed orders from first order through assignment | at | input |
| average_order_value | Lifetime spend divided by lifetime order count, handled safely when there is no order history | at | input |
| marketing_consent_flag | Whether the buyer can be contacted in the intended channel | at | input |
| preferred_channel | Buyer’s current opt-in or highest-performing contact channel | at | input |
| email_engagement_rate | Opens or clicks per valid email sent up to assignment | at | input |
| recent_cart_flag | Whether the buyer added an item to cart without purchase inside the chosen pre-assignment window | at | input |
| recent_category_interest | Category purchased, added, or viewed inside the chosen pre-assignment window | at | input |
| next_order_flag | Completed order in the chosen post-assignment observation window | after | label |
| next_period_spend | Revenue from completed orders in the chosen post-assignment observation window | after | label |

Each row is a buyer-state snapshot: one buyer observed at one cohort assignment date.  
The moment of the decision is the buyer’s `cohort_assignment_date`, when the lifecycle team chooses the cohort and the associated action.  
The label is defined as buyer behavior after assignment: `next_order_flag` means the buyer completed an order in the chosen post-assignment observation window, and it is known only after that window closes; `next_period_spend` is the revenue from orders in that same window.

## Model
Begin with a simple baseline before using a model: rule-based RFM segmentation. Score each buyer by `days_since_last_order`, `order_count_in_lookback`, and `spend_in_lookback`, then assign them to ordered tiers using the business’s own threshold definitions or the distribution of their existing data. This baseline should be transparent and directly routeable to lifecycle offers.

After the baseline exists, build a behavioral cohort model using clustering on standardized buyer-state features: recency, frequency, value, email engagement, cart abandonment, category interest, and channel preference. A simple first model is k-means or a Gaussian mixture model, because both are easy to inspect and map to named lifecycle segments. The model should be fit only on features known at `cohort_assignment_date`.

To test it, split by time rather than randomly. Use earlier assignment dates as training snapshots and later assignment dates as validation snapshots. This mirrors how lifecycle marketing actually works: the team must assign cohorts for future buyers using data available at the decision date. On the validation snapshots, apply the model and compare the resulting cohorts with the RFM baseline using the labels `next_order_flag` and `next_period_spend`. Also inspect whether cohorts remain stable over time and whether each cohort is large enough to justify its own offer.

The model score becomes the decision in three steps: each buyer receives a cohort ID, each cohort ID is reviewed by the lifecycle team to create a name and action, and the assigned action is pushed to CRM or email. If the model’s cohorts cannot be mapped clearly to lifecycle actions, keep the simpler RFM rule-based approach until the operational value is clear.

## Plan
1. Define the cohort decision. Decide what lifecycle action the cohort must drive, who owns it, and when buyers are assigned. This can be done this week without data. Finish when you have a written decision moment and a list of cohort names.
2. Agree the buyer snapshot. Define that the unit is one buyer at one `cohort_assignment_date`, not one order, not one session, and not one email campaign. Finish when the data model uses buyer-date rows.
3. Specify the features. Confirm which fields above exist: order recency, order frequency, spend, email engagement, cart activity, category interest, and consent status. Finish when each feature has a source table and an owner.

6. Measure the baseline. For historical assignment dates, compute `next_order_flag` and `next_period_spend` by cohort and compare them with current campaign performance. Finish when you know whether the baseline cohorts separate business outcomes.
7. Build the model version. Fit the clustering model on training snapshots and evaluate it on later snapshots. Finish when the model cohorts are validated against the baseline and against future labels.
8. Deploy with monitoring. Assign cohorts to campaigns and monitor cohort stability, offer performance, opt-out risk, and revenue per campaign. Finish when the lifecycle team can make campaign decisions from the cohort output without needing to re-derive them manually.

Real data will show which features actually exist and are clean enough to use. It will settle the right lookback windows, the threshold ranges for recency, frequency, and value, and whether buyer behavior is separable into meaningful cohorts. It will show how many cohorts are useful, whether the model adds value over the RFM baseline, which cohorts are stable over time, and how much lift exists for each lifecycle action. Without your data, any specific window, threshold, cohort count, or expected performance would be invented rather than earned.

Our hospital wants to predict at the moment of patient discharge whether a patient will be readmitted within 30 days. Because of HIPAA privacy rules we cannot upload patient records. We discharge 3,000 patients a month with a 12% readmission rate; a follow-up nurse visit costs $80 and avoids a $1,600 penalty.

## What the problem is

The real decision is not just “will this patient be readmitted?” but “should this discharge get a follow-up nurse visit?” That makes it a predictive triage problem.

**Given by you:**

- The prediction point is the moment of patient discharge.
- The outcome of interest is readmission within 30 days.
- HIPAA privacy rules prevent uploading patient records elsewhere.
- Your hospital discharges 3,000 patients a month.
- The current readmission rate is 12%.
- A follow-up nurse visit costs $80.
- A nurse visit can avoid a $1,600 penalty.

**What the result is for:**

- Discharge planners, care managers, nursing leaders, quality managers, and financial/penalty-management staff.
- The result should help them decide which patients to reach with a nurse follow-up visit.

**What the unit is:**

- One discharged patient, or more precisely one discharge episode.
- The decision must be made before or at discharge, when the nurse-visit decision still can be influenced.

**What is known:**

- The hospital has a discharge volume and a readmission baseline.
- There is a clear cost for intervention and a clear avoided penalty if intervention works.
- The prediction must be done inside your protected environment because patient records cannot be uploaded.

**What is not known from your message:**

- What data fields are available at discharge: diagnoses, prior admissions, lab values, vital signs, medications, insurance, social risk, care-team notes, etc.
- Whether the 12% readmission rate includes all readmissions or only penalty-eligible readmissions.
- Whether nurse visits truly avoid the penalty, or whether avoided penalties come from other post-discharge care actions.
- Whether all patients have contact information needed for nurse follow-up.
- Whether your hospital has limited nurse-visit capacity, or whether the question is purely value-based targeting.
- Whether the hospital already uses some follow-up protocol and, if so, what it is.
- Whether retrospective outcomes can be linked back to discharge records locally.

**Important assumptions that should be checked:**

- The penalty applies when a readmission occurs but would have been avoided by the nurse visit.
- The nurse visit has a meaningful chance of changing the outcome, rather than merely documenting an outcome that was going to happen anyway.
- The hospital can build and run the model internally without exporting patient-level records.
- Predicted risk can be converted into a practical action: assign nurse follow-up to higher-value patients.

---

## Possible approaches

### Approach 1: No model at all

You could ignore prediction and either:

- Give nurse visits to every discharged patient.
- Give nurse visits to a random subset.
- Give nurse visits based on a simple checklist, such as prior admissions, certain discharge diagnoses, or care-team judgment.

**What this costs:**

- Very little technical development.
- Easy to explain and operate.
- But possibly high nurse-visit cost if applied broadly, and possibly poor penalty avoidance if applied without targeting.

**What this gives:**

- A practical baseline.
- Immediate action without needing model validation.
- A reference point for comparing whether a predictive model is actually worth building.

**Why this matters:**

A model should be built only if it helps choose who gets the visit better than the simplest current practice.

---

### Approach 2: Simple clinical risk rule

This would use a small number of clearly understandable risk factors, such as:

- Recent prior admission.
- Certain high-risk discharge diagnoses.
- Length of stay.
- Number of active medications.
- Missing follow-up appointment at discharge.
- Care-team flagged complexity.

The rule would assign some patients to nurse follow-up and others not.

**What this costs:**

- Low to moderate data effort.
- Needs agreement from clinicians and quality staff.
- Needs periodic review as practice changes.

**What this gives:**

- Transparent prioritization.
- Easy HIPAA-safe implementation inside your hospital.
- Useful when the team needs something immediately before a full model is ready.

**Limitations:**

- It may miss interactions between risk factors.
- It may not identify the highest economic value patients unless it is carefully calibrated to outcome risk.

---

### Approach 3: Logistic regression risk model

This is a statistical model that estimates the probability of 30-day readmission using patient features available at discharge.

**What this costs:**

- Needs clean historical discharge data with linked 30-day readmission outcomes.
- Needs local computing or a privacy-preserving environment.
- Needs a validation period before go-live.
- Needs periodic monitoring and retraining.

**What this gives:**

- A ranked list of discharge episodes by predicted readmission risk.
- Interpretable coefficients or risk factors if built carefully.
- A way to combine many weak signals into one decision score.
- A foundation for expected-value targeting: use risk score, visit cost, and penalty avoided to decide who gets follow-up.

**Why this is attractive:**

It is simple enough for hospital operations, defensible clinically, and does not require sending patient records outside your environment.

---

### Approach 4: Tree-based or gradient-boosted machine-learning model

This type of model can capture more complex patterns in the data, such as interactions among age, diagnoses, prior admissions, discharge medications, and social factors.

**What this costs:**

- More data preparation.
- More validation.
- More explanation work, because clinicians may need to understand why a patient was flagged.
- More monitoring, because complex models can drift when patient mix, policies, or staff behavior changes.

**What this gives:**

- Potentially better prediction than logistic regression.
- Potentially better targeting of nurse visits.
- More robust handling of mixed feature types and nonlinear relationships.

**Limitations:**

- It may be harder to trust clinically if not explained well.
- It may add little if the simple logistic model already captures the main risk signals.

---

### Approach 5: Survival model over 30 days

Instead of predicting only whether readmission happens within 30 days, this could estimate how soon the risk appears after discharge.

**What this costs:**

- More complex modeling.
- Needs timing of readmissions, not just whether readmission happened.

**What this gives:**

- A more nuanced view of when intervention may be most useful.
- Potentially better sequencing of nurse outreach.

**Limitations:**

- Your stated decision is mostly about who gets a post-discharge nurse visit, not exactly when.
- It may add complexity without adding much operational value unless timing is a real constraint.

---

### Approach 6: Causal or uplift model

A standard risk model predicts who is likely to be readmitted. That is useful, but the true business question is who will benefit from the nurse visit and who will not be readmitted because of it.

An uplift model tries to predict treatment effect: the difference in readmission probability between getting the nurse visit and not getting it.

**What this costs:**

- Needs historical data showing which patients did or did not receive nurse visits.
- Needs careful handling of confounding: sicker patients may already have been chosen for visits.
- Needs clinical and operational review of the intervention process.

**What this gives:**

- Potentially the most economically correct targeting: not just “highest risk,” but “highest risk reduction from the visit.”
- Avoids wasting visits on patients who would not be readmitted anyway or would be readmitted regardless.

**Limitations:**

- Harder to build and validate.
- Requires the intervention to have measurable causal effect in your actual setting.
- May be premature as a first project.

---

### Approach 7: Decision-only targeting model

This starts not with “what is the best readmission model?” but with “what action gives the best financial and clinical value?”

Because the nurse visit costs $80 and can avoid a $1,600 penalty, the targeting logic should compare the value of avoided penalties with the cost of visits.

**What this costs:**

- Needs a way to estimate expected avoided penalty from predicted risk and intervention effectiveness.
- Needs an operational assumption about how many visits your nurse team can provide.
- Needs monitoring of whether predicted value matches realized value.

**What this gives:**

- A business-oriented model that directly supports the decision to allocate nurse visits.
- A clearer connection between prediction, intervention, and cost saving.

---

## Recommended approach

I would choose a **local logistic regression readmission risk model with an expected-value targeting rule**.

That means:

- Build the model inside your hospital’s protected environment, so patient records are not uploaded.
- Predict probability of 30-day readmission at discharge.
- Use that risk score to rank discharge episodes.
- Prioritize nurse visits by expected value, using the given visit cost of $80 and the given avoided penalty of $1,600.
- Keep the model simple enough for clinicians and administrators to trust and operate.

This is better than starting with a complex machine-learning or causal model because you can get practical value quickly, validate it against real discharge decisions, and then add sophistication only if needed.

---

## Plan for the chosen approach

### Define the target clearly

The target should be: readmission within 30 days of discharge.

Need to confirm:

- Which types of readmission count.
- Whether observation stays, emergency department visits without admission, transfers between facilities, or planned readmissions should be included or excluded.
- Whether the penalty target is the same as the readmission target.

If the penalty applies to a narrower subset than all readmissions, the model should predict the penalty-eligible outcome, not only general readmission.

---

### Confirm privacy-preserving implementation

Because patient records cannot be uploaded, the model must be built and run locally, or inside a secure enclave that your hospital controls.

Need to define:

- Where data will be stored.
- Who can access it.
- How model outputs are shared with staff.
- Whether only aggregate metrics can leave the hospital.
- How audit logs and access controls will work.

This should be treated as a design requirement, not an afterthought.

---

### Build the historical dataset

You need a training dataset made of past discharge episodes.

For each discharge episode, collect only information available at the discharge moment.

Possible features could include:

- Age.
- Sex or gender, if permitted and useful.
- Prior admission history.
- Length of stay.
- Discharge diagnosis.
- Comorbidities.
- Number of medications.
- High-risk medication classes.
- Vital signs near discharge.
- Lab values near discharge.
- Emergency department history.
- Insurance or payer type.
- Social risk indicators, if available.
- Care-team flags.
- Follow-up appointment status.
- Discharge destination.

Need to avoid leakage:

- Do not use information recorded after discharge.
- Do not use information that was only discovered because of the readmission itself.
- Do not include nurse-visit assignment as a feature if that visit is meant to be the intervention being targeted.

---

### Define the outcome labels

Match each past discharge episode to whether the patient was readmitted within 30 days.

Need to confirm:

- The timing rule for 30-day readmission.
- Whether the readmission can be to any hospital or must be local.
- Whether transfers count.
- Whether planned readmissions count.
- Whether mortality is treated differently.

Label quality is critical. A model built on poorly defined readmission outcomes can be misleading.

---

### Create baseline comparisons

Before judging the model, compare it with simple baselines:

- No follow-up.
- Follow-up for all patients.
- Follow-up based on current care-team judgment.
- Follow-up based on the 12% readmission baseline.
- A simple clinical risk rule.

These baselines tell you whether the model adds value beyond what your team already does.

---

### Fit the logistic risk model

The model estimates the probability of 30-day readmission from features known at discharge.

The model should be built to be:

- Calibrated: predicted risk should match observed risk.
- Interpretable: clinicians should understand what raises or lowers risk.
- Stable over time: performance should not collapse when patient mix changes.
- Operationally usable: scores can be produced at discharge and used in workflow.

A gradient-boosted model can be compared later, but logistic regression is a good starting point because it is easier to explain and defend.

---

### Separate risk prediction from intervention value

A high-risk patient may not always be the best target if the nurse visit cannot meaningfully change their outcome. But without causal intervention data, the practical first version can target the patients with the highest expected avoided-penalty value.

For each discharge episode:

- Use predicted readmission probability.
- Consider whether the nurse visit is available.
- Estimate expected avoided penalty.
- Compare that value with the $80 visit cost.
- Rank patients by expected net value.

This turns prediction into a decision rule instead of just a dashboard.

---

### Add operational constraints

The model should reflect real capacity.

Need to know:

- How many nurse visits the team can realistically provide.
- Whether visits can be given before discharge, same-day, or after discharge.
- Whether some patients cannot be contacted.
- Whether clinical priority should override predicted value.
- Whether the team wants a fixed list per day or a flexible threshold.

If there is no capacity limit, then the rule can simply include all patients whose expected value exceeds cost. If there is a limit, the model should rank them and select the top eligible patients up to that limit.

---

### Validate on unseen time periods

Do not only test on old data from the same period. The best validation is time-based:

- Train on earlier discharge episodes.
- Validate on later discharge episodes.
- Test on an untouched recent period.

Need to check:

- How well the model separates high-risk from lower-risk patients.
- Whether predicted probabilities are accurate, not just the ranking.
- Whether performance is stable across different days, seasons, units, or patient types.
- Whether any group is being systematically under- or over-selected.

---

### Measure decision value, not just model accuracy

The final test is whether the nurse-visit targeting works.

Compare these strategies:

- Current practice.
- Simple clinical rule.
- Logistic model targeting.
- Model plus expected-value rule.

For each strategy, estimate:

- Number of nurse visits given.
- Visit costs.
- Readmissions avoided.
- Penalties avoided.
- Net operational value.
- Clinician acceptance.
- False positives, meaning visits given to patients who likely would not need them.
- Missed high-value patients.

The key question is not “what is the best model score?” but “what is the best value from using the model to decide who gets follow-up?”

---

### Run a controlled pilot before full rollout

Before changing the discharge process everywhere, run a limited pilot.

The pilot should be:

- Time-limited.
- Unit-limited or team-limited.
- Clearly documented.
- Compared against current practice.
- Monitored for clinical safety.
- Monitored for whether staff actually follow the recommendations.

Need to check:

- Does staff trust the recommendations?
- Are patients actually reachable for nurse visits?
- Are visits delivered quickly enough?
- Are avoided penalties happening as expected?
- Are some patients flagged too often or too rarely?

---

### Monitor continuously

After deployment, keep watching:

- Model calibration.
- Feature availability.
- Changes in patient mix.
- Changes in discharge protocols.
- Changes in readmission rules.
- Changes in penalty logic.
- Nurse-visit effectiveness.
- Staff override behavior.

Retrain or recalibrate when performance drifts or when operations change.

---

## When to stop or change the approach

Stop expanding the project if:

- The model does not beat the simple clinical baseline.
- The expected-value targeting does not improve nurse-visit allocation.
- The data are too inconsistent or incomplete to build a reliable risk score.
- Clinicians cannot use the output in the discharge workflow.
- HIPAA or security requirements prevent local deployment in a practical way.
- The nurse visits do not actually avoid penalties, meaning the predicted financial benefit is not realized.
- The model flags patients who cannot realistically be reached or helped.

Change the approach if:

- Logistic regression is too weak and the data support a better model.
- The hospital has historical data showing nurse visits are effective only for some patient groups, in which case an uplift or causal model may become worth building.
- The main issue is timing of outreach rather than patient selection, in which case a survival-style or sequencing model may help.
- The penalty rules differ from general readmission rules, in which case the model should be refocused on penalty-eligible readmission.

---

## Bottom recommendation

Start with a **local, interpretable logistic regression model** that predicts 30-day readmission at discharge. Do not send patient records outside your hospital. Do not treat model accuracy as the final goal. Treat the final goal as **better nurse-visit targeting using the $80 visit cost and the $1,600 avoided penalty as the business logic**.

Before building anything complex, confirm:

- The exact readmission outcome definition.
- The exact penalty-eligibility definition.
- The nurse-visit capacity.
- The data available at discharge without leakage.
- Whether current practice already captures the main value.

If the simple model and decision rule beat current practice in a pilot, it deserves wider use. If it does not, a simple rule or targeted process improvement may be the better answer.

The unit is each machine, considered at a current decision time, over a 7-day horizon.

What you told me:
- There are 1,200 industrial compressors.
- You want failure prediction 7 days before breakdown.
- Sensor logging has not started yet.
- A preventive inspection costs $120.
- That inspection can avoid $3,000 of unplanned downtime.

What I assume unless you correct me:
- The decision is machine-by-machine.
- An inspection is useful only when it correctly triggers preventive maintenance.
- The inspection cost is paid for each inspection performed.
- The avoided cost is credited when a real failure is prevented.

What is not known:
- Which failure modes matter most.
- Which sensors would give usable early signals.
- Whether you already have maintenance logs, failure labels, downtime records, manufacturer guidance, or calendar-based preventive schedules.
- The baseline failure rate.
- Whether every failure is preventable by inspection.
- How many inspections the maintenance team can actually perform.
- Whether the $3,000 downtime value is fixed for every machine or varies by machine, process, or outage length.

Approaches that could solve it:

No model at all: reactive maintenance.
- Cost: inspections are not triggered by risk, so they may be skipped until failure happens.
- Gives: the simplest baseline, because it shows how much downtime cost occurs when no action is taken.
- Trade-off: if failures are rare and preventable, this may be cheaper than many inspections; if failures are common or disruptive, it may be too costly.

Time-based or calendar-based preventive inspection.
- Cost: inspections are paid for on a fixed schedule, whether or not a machine is actually failing.
- Gives: a no-data baseline that may reduce failures if wear is age-related or time-related.
- Trade-off: it may spend $120 on many low-risk machines while still missing condition-driven failures.

Existing maintenance-log risk ranking, if any records exist.
- Cost: needs access to past repair, inspection, downtime, or manufacturer records; little new modeling.
- Gives: a simple ranking based on age, service history, past alarms, or known failure patterns.
- Trade-off: without sensor data, the signal may be weak, and it cannot capture early physical failure signs.

Condition-based rules after starting sensor logging.
- Cost: requires installing or connecting sensors, logging data, storing history, and defining thresholds.
- Gives: practical alerts from known indicators such as pressure, temperature, vibration, current, flow, duty cycle, or usage hours.
- Trade-off: rules need expert tuning and may miss subtle or multivariate failures.

Predictive machine learning after enough data exists.
- Cost: needs a meaningful history of sensor readings and labeled failures; needs data engineering, labeling, validation, model training, deployment, and ongoing monitoring.
- Gives: a probability that a machine will fail within 7 days, which can be converted into an inspection decision using the $120 cost and $3,000 avoided cost.
- Trade-off: this is expensive and may be unnecessary if simple rules or maintenance logs do not show usable signal. It also fails early if failures are rare or sensor data is noisy.

My chosen approach: start with data collection and a no-model baseline, not a predictive model.

Because sensor logging has not started, a failure prediction model cannot be trained yet. The best first plan is to make the measurement system and decision economics clear, then use the simplest workable rule.

Steps:

- Define exactly what counts as a failure: an unplanned compressor breakdown that causes downtime.
- Define the 7-day horizon from the time a decision is made.
- Decide whether the prediction means “will fail during the next 7 days from now” or “will fail within 7 days from the last sensor reading.” This matters for how labels are created.

Confirm the decision rule.
- Treat each alert as a cost decision.
- An alert is worth acting on only when the expected avoided downtime exceeds the expected inspection cost.
- In practical terms: true failures caught should generate $3,000 of avoided downtime per prevented failure, while every inspection consumes $120, including inspections triggered by false alerts.

Choose the sensors and failure indicators.
- Work with reliability engineers or maintenance technicians to identify the most likely compressor failure modes.
- Start logging the smallest useful set of signals: pressure, temperature, vibration, electrical current, flow, runtime, start-stop counts, and maintenance or alarm events.
- The sensor set may differ by machine type; the goal is not to collect everything, but to collect signals likely tied to failure.

Start logging with a machine identifier and time.
- Create a table structure now, even before values are meaningful.
- Each row should be tied to a specific machine and timestamp.
- Keep enough history to understand both normal operation and the lead-up to failure.
- Store maintenance actions separately from sensor readings.
